name: Finnish
variety: Standard Finnish (yleiskieli); duration figures are from educated speakers from Jyväskylä (Lehtonen 1970)
sources: Suomi, Kari; Toivanen, Juhani; Ylitalo, Riikka (2008). Finnish Sound Structure: Phonetics, Phonology, Phonotactics and Prosody. Studia Humaniora Ouluensia 9. Oulu University Press.
Lehtonen, Jaakko (1970). Aspects of Quantity in Standard Finnish. Studia Philologica Jyväskyläensia VI. University of Jyväskylä.
Wiik, Kalevi (1965). Finnish and English Vowels. Annales Universitatis Turkuensis B 94. Turku.
Iivonen, Antti; Harnud, Huhe (2005). Acoustical comparison of the monophthong systems in Finnish, Mongolian and Udmurt. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 35(1): 59-71.
Suomi, Kari (1980). Voicing in English and Finnish Stops. Publications of the Department of Finnish and General Linguistics of the University of Turku.
Suomi, Kari; Toivanen, Juhani; Ylitalo, Riikka (2003). Durational and tonal correlates of accent in Finnish. Journal of Phonetics 31: 113-138.
Iivonen, Antti (1998). Intonation in Finnish. In Hirst, Daniel & Di Cristo, Albert (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Nakai, Satsuki; Kunnari, Sari; Turk, Alice; Suomi, Kari; Ylitalo, Riikka (2009). Utterance-final lengthening and quantity in Northern Finnish. Journal of Phonetics 37(1).
Nakai, Satsuki; Suomi, Kari; Wrench, Alan (2015). F1/F2 targets for Finnish single vs. double vowels. Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Glasgow.
Horslund, Camilla Søballe (2019). VOT in loanwords in Finnish: evidence for prevoicing of initial /b, d, g/. Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Melbourne.
Karlsson, Fred (1999). Finnish: An Essential Grammar. Routledge.
contrasts: vowel length (single versus double) for all eight vowels, in stressed and unstressed syllables alike
consonant length (single versus geminate) for /p t k s m n l r/; /ŋ/ between vowels is always long [ŋː]
three-way vowel series: front unrounded /i e æ/, front rounded /y ø/, back /u o ɑ/
eighteen diphthongs contrasting with vowel sequences split by a syllable boundary
no voicing contrast in native stops apart from /t̪/ versus /d/; /b ɡ f ʃ/ occur only in loanwords
allophony: /h/ is breathy voiced [ɦ] between voiced sounds, [ç] in a syllable coda after a high front vowel (vihko) and [x] in a coda after a back vowel (kahvi)
/n/ takes the place of a following stop within words and across word boundaries: [m] before labials, [ŋ] before velars
/ŋ/ occurs only before /k/ and as geminate [ŋː] (written ng)
/t̪/ is dental, /d/ is alveolar with a short, often tap-like closure
/s/ is often retracted [s̠] and varies widely because no native /ʃ/ contrasts with it
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant with little or no friction
a single vowel in the second syllable after a light first syllable (CV.CV) is half-long: about 105 ms against about 48 ms after a heavy first syllable (Lehtonen 1970)
single vowels are somewhat more central in quality than double vowels, an effect of their short duration (Nakai, Suomi & Wrench 2015)
a glottal stop or creak can separate vowels at word boundaries and appears where boundary gemination meets a vowel-initial word
phonotactics: vowel harmony: within a non-compound native word the back vowels /ɑ o u/ do not combine with the front vowels /æ ø y/; /i e/ are neutral
native words have no initial consonant clusters and end in a vowel or in /t s n r l/

boundary gemination: certain word forms (nouns in -e such as vene, second person imperatives, first infinitives, connegative verbs, allative -lle and others) lengthen the first consonant of the following word or clitic
the opening diphthongs /ie uo yø/ occur only in the first syllable
/d/ occurs only word-medially in native words, mostly as the weak grade of /t̪/
/b ɡ f ʃ/ occur only in loanwords and are often replaced by /p k ʋ s/ in colloquial speech

stress.rule: Primary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word; secondary stress falls on the third syllable, or on the fourth if the third is light and the fourth heavy, and then on every second syllable, the final syllable normally staying unstressed.
stress.cues: segmental lengthening over the first two morae of the word and the alignment of the phrasal rise-fall pitch movement; intensity is a weak cue, vowel quality does not change, and duration is mainly reserved for the quantity contrast

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: unstressed vowels keep their quality and the length contrast; short vowels are only slightly centralised
rhythm.notes: Traditionally called syllable-timed, but timing is organised by the mora and the two-syllable foot. Utterance-final lengthening is restricted so that the quantity contrast survives (Nakai et al. 2009).

length.notes: First-syllable double vowels are about 2.2 times as long as single vowels: means 153 ms against 70 ms in words read in sentence frames (Lehtonen 1970); Wiik (1965) found 1 : 2.3. In later syllables the ratio is 1 : 2.2 to 1 : 3.2, except that a single second-syllable vowel after a light first syllable is half-long, giving only 1 : 1.4 to 1 : 1.5. Geminate consonants between the first and second syllable average 158 ms against 78 ms for singles (ratio 1 : 2.0): /p/ 97 and 194 ms, /t/ 88 and 186, /k/ 105 and 194, /s/ 81 and 163; sonorants have a larger ratio of about 1 : 2.5: /n/ 47 and 123 ms, /l/ 49 and 118, /r/ 42 and 103 (Lehtonen 1970, tables 9 to 11).

voice_onset_time_ms.notes: Horslund (2019) measured somewhat longer values in young speakers and found the loanword stops /b d ɡ/ prevoiced for most but not all speakers (means across 11 speakers about -37, -51 and -23 ms).

intonation.declarative: gradual fall through the utterance; each accented word has a rise-fall on its first two morae, the peaks declining step by step; the end is low and often creaky or breathy
intonation.yes_no_question: no final rise as a rule: the question is marked by the clitic -ko/-kö on the fronted word and the contour falls as in a statement, often from a higher start
intonation.wh_question: high on the initial question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: level or slightly rising pitch, or a suspended fall, at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: LHL: rise on the stressed first syllable with the peak near the end of the first or on the second mora, followed by a fall
intonation.notes: Final rises occur in some styles and in younger urban speech but are not the unmarked pattern.

tone.notes: No lexical tone or pitch accent.

phonation: creaky or breathy voice and devoicing towards the end of utterances
breathy voiced [ɦ] for /h/ between voiced sounds

problems: /h/ has a single realisation: no [x] or [ç] in syllable codas (kahvi, vihko, lahti) and no voiced [ɦ] between vowels
unstressed /i/ is replaced by a laxer vowel (phoneme I, printed [ɪ]) through ChangeIfUnstressed, although Finnish has no vowel reduction

boundary gemination is applied only after a short word list and four endings (fi_list $double; -lle, -nne, -sti, -tse); it is missing for most -e nouns, imperatives and infinitives and inside compounds (hernekeitto has single [k])
questions get a rising tune (intonation group 3 maps the question mark to the fall-rise 'comma' tune), whereas Finnish questions normally fall
the half-long second-syllable vowel after a light first syllable (tuli, kala) is not modelled; all single vowels have one length

length ratios are only approximated: a geminate stop adds a fixed 130 ms of closure (long_stop) and other geminates repeat the consonant, so the larger ratio for sonorants (about 1 : 2.5) and the position effects are not reproduced
single and double vowels share one formant target, so the more central quality of short vowels is absent
no utterance-final creaky or breathy voice
good: fixed initial stress with quantity-sensitive secondary stress (secondary stress moves from a light to a following heavy syllable)
vowel and consonant length are both represented
all eighteen diphthongs have their own phonemes
nasal place assimilation within and across words, and ng as [ŋː]
dental /t/, alveolar /d/ and approximant /ʋ/ are distinguished from the base-table sounds

notes: Vowel formant values are left out: Wiik (1965) and Iivonen & Harnud (2005) give them, but the figures could not be checked for this profile.
